title.narrative: Australia-Indonesia Partnership Towards an Inclusive Society

description.narrative: Australia Indonesia Partnership Towards an Inclusive Society or also known as INKLUSI. INKLUSI continues Australia’s support to Indonesia’s prosperity, building on advancements in the areas of gender equality and women’s empowerment, disability rights, social inclusion and civil society strengthening. INKLUSI aims to empower civil society organisations (CSOs) and facilitate collaboration with the Indonesian Government at national and sub-national levels to contribute to the broader development goal of: No one is left behind - More marginalised people participate in and benefit from decisions about Indonesia’ sociocultural, economic and political development.

Australia Indonesia Partnership Towards an Inclusive Society (INKLUSI) Midterm Review

description.narrative: Australia supported Civil Society Organisation (CSO) partners building on their expertise and experiences to establish and manage 244 community-based services and strengthen their network with other service providers. For examples, Aisyiyah, a supported CSO, established community-based centres, Balai Sakinah, worked with the government and its referral services providers including the Family Learning Centres and Public Health Centres, to deliver services to women including to women with disability. On policy, KAPAL Perempuan, another supported CSO made progress towards systemic change to protect survivors of violence through their role in the Government-established team to accelerate implementation of the Law on Sexual Violence.

Australia's partnership with SIGAB, a disability rights organisation is providing support to the disability community. INKLUSI supported SIGAB's transition into a grant-making entity and upgraded its financial systems, enhancing partnerships with local disability organisations. This collaboration expanded SIGAB's network, establishing links with central government, CSOs, the private sector, and universities. Australia provided grant funding, training, audit capacity building, and networking opportunities, enabling SIGAB to strengthen 62 Village Disability Groups. These groups advocate for disability inclusion in decision-making processes and facilitate the development of accessible infrastructure, supported by economic initiatives from district governments.

Australia's CSO partners have established community-based groups to handle cases of violence, focusing on gender equality, sexual violence, and gender-based violence. These groups supported 773 victims/survivors, addressing issues such as child marriage, domestic violence, and harassment (including against transgender individuals). They provided initial advice and referrals to local government services (UPTD PPA) and other CSOs, including emergency shelters, psychosocial support, healthcare, police, legal aid, and court proceedings. BaKTI, an INKLUSI partner, strengthened seven Regional Technical Implementation Units for Women and Children's Protection (UPTD PPA) to strengthen government’s response to violence against women and children

Australia's CSO partners utilised flexible grant funding to assist 5,697 marginalised individuals (including 2,190 males, 3,401 females, 1,161 of them are people with disabilities) in accessing social protection. They achieved this by establishing community-based groups and enhancing their capacity to provide referral mechanisms. CSO partners also directly facilitated access to social protection services. For instance, PEKKA’s KLIK PEKKA clinics and paralegals collaborated with local agencies, resulting in 675 instances of access to government programs. BaKTI’s Constituent Groups (Kelompok Konstituen) facilitated 2,929 cases by leveraging official recognition to resolve social protection issues directly with district authorities through village decrees and identification cards.

Australian grant funding through the Australia Indonesia Partnership Towards an Inclusive Society has empowered local civil society organisation (CSO) partners in Indonesia to support 3,290 women entrepreneurs (including 7 with disabilities) to establish and enhance their businesses and cooperatives. Capacity building provided includes business management skills, business licensing, financial management, and marketing to access markets. CSOs facilitated access to economic programs and support from government and NGOs. Australia’s CSO partner PEKKA's Paradigta Entrepreneurship Academy trained 1,586 women in leadership, advocacy, and business management, resulting in new ventures. For instance, in Jruek Bale village, Aceh Besar District, a woman launched an embroidery group serving an international company, doubling her income and creating opportunities for others.

IAusralia's CSO partners collaborated with the National Development Planning Agency (Bappenas) and the Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and Child Protection (KemenPPA) to advocate for Gender Equality, Diversity, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI) integration in Indonesia's 2025-2045 Long Term Development Plan (RPJPN). GEDSI principles are now integrated throughout the plan, signalling government commitment to inclusive policies. Australia and its partners facilitated the National Women’s Conference for Development Planning, engaging 4,423 women to inform RPJPN recommendations across 9 key areas

INKLUSI CSO partners’ engagement with 24 district governments and 82 private sector organisations contributed to greater employment of people with disability. CSO partners supported the establishment and/or strengthening of 24 Disability Services Units (ULD) to promote disability employment. They built government awareness and commitment and provided technical assistance to support ULD’s mandate. This included engaging the private sector to support their national target of allocating at least 1% of employment opportunities to people with disability. ‍ In Cirebon District, West Java, INKLUSI’s CSOs SIGAB and FKDC supported passage of the Cirebon District Disability Regulation in April 2024, which strengthens the role of ULDs and expands access to vocational and entrepreneurship training. In collaboration with the ULD, they trained 50 companies on inclusion of GEDSI principles and labour regulations related to disability. This led to companies formally committing to employ people with disability, improving workplace accessibility and reporting disability employment data transparently. FKDC also facilitated GEDSI workshops with local government’s representatives. The Cirebon ULD reported FKDC’s support enabled 651 people with disability to gain employment across 27 companies - 50 of whom were directly supported by FKDC. These efforts have helped shift corporate mindsets toward inclusion, equity, and respect in the workplace.

INKLUSI is catalysing inclusive policy and practice across Indonesia to support women and marginalised people to participate in and benefit from Indonesia’s development. Its grant funding and capacity-building has strengthened the GEDSI focus and GEDSI approaches of national and local CSO partners. These CSO partners collaborate with the Indonesian government on inclusive policies, including: ‍ -Integrating GEDSI into national and local government long-term, medium-term and annual development planning. ‍ -Strengthening disability inclusion, through development of national and regional action plans and district and village regulations; implementing government initiatives for inclusive villages in 182 villages; inclusive education and employment of people with disability; and strengthening services to better meet the needs of people with disability (including people with psychosocial disability). ‍ -Establishing and strengthening Regional Technical Implementation Units for Protection of Women and Children to prevent and respond to cases of violence against women and children. ‍ -Accelerating prevention of child marriage, through building government awareness, developing legal frameworks and strengthening services to prevent and handle cases of child marriage. ‍ INKLUSI’s CSO partners also established and strengthened taskforces to prevent and respond to sexual violence in university campuses and built the awareness and capacity of private sector leading to more employment of people with disability.

INKLUSI supports women and marginalised people to participate in and benefit from Indonesia’s development. To achieve this, INKLUSI provided flexible grants to five national women’s CSOs to collaborate with 75 local women’s organisations to empower women and marginalised people, in line with their organisational strengths and mandates. ‍ Through a diverse set of initiatives, these women’s organisations are driving more inclusive development across Indonesia, ensuring benefits reach women and marginalised people. In 2024-25, they: ‍ •established 216 community groups which have provided services to 34,416 women and marginalised people ‍ •through advocacy, facilitation and community group referrals, enabled 15,878 women and marginalised people to access government services ‍ •supported 4,379 women and marginalised people to participate in public decision-making processes ‍ •supported the establishment of 1,400 economic groups (businesses and cooperatives) involving 8,413 women and marginalised people; and ‍ •supported the development of more inclusive government policies from the national to village level. ‍ INKLUSI’s flexible funding, capacity-building and convening continues to enable the national CSOs to strengthen their organisational capacity, including related to GEDSI, networks, policy advocacy, monitoring evaluation and learning, grant management and safeguards. Through enhanced capacity-building of local women’s organisations, they are building a stronger women’s movement.

INKLUSI’s CSO national partner ‘Aisyiyah has supported marginalised women—including elderly women and women with disabilities—to establish and strengthen 119 businesses during the reporting period. These businesses include food processing, handicrafts, eco-batik, poultry, and home-based snack production. Through skills training, business formalisation (including licences and product certification), start-up capital and financial literacy, ‘Aisyiyah has helped women gain confidence and economic independence. ‍ One inspiring example is Lena, a mother of a child with a disability in Tasikmalaya district, West Java. Initially she joined a training program and received seed support from ‘Aisyiyah’s women’s group, Balai Sakinah Aisyiyah (BSA). Through BSA, Lena became actively involved in a nutrition garden project with other BSA members. She applied her new knowledge at home, starting a backyard food garden, processing cassava into a range of chips, and raising chickens. ‍ When her husband fell ill, Lena became the family’s breadwinner, relying on her enterprise skills to meet household needs for a year. The training and book-keeping skills boosted her confidence to grow her business. With her success, her previously unemployed husband joined in. Lena now inspires other women in her village to start businesses, showing how inclusive, community-led support can empower individuals and drive resilience.

INKLUSI’s CSO partner PERMAMPU (a consortium of 8 CSOs operating across Sumatra, including Women’s Crisis Centres or WCC) established 31 One Stop Service and Learning (OSS&L), based in Community Health Centers (Puskesmas). These OSS&L provide vital services for women and children victims of violence, especially in rural and marginalised communities. ‍ In 2024-25, PERMAMPU trained 556 grassroots women to become OSS&L community cadres who are offering initial support and referrals. These cadres are the first responders for women and child victims, helping them report and document their cases and providing initial psychosocial support. They also play a crucial role in referrals to official services such as the local government’s Regional Technical Implementation Units for Protection of Women and Children (UPTD PPA) and PERMAMPU members’ WCC. These WCC enable victims to access vital services, including shelter, trauma counselling, medical and forensic services, and legal aid—such as assistance with police reports, court hearings, and follow-up on court decisions. ‍ During this reporting period, 281 women and children have accessed support services from OSS&L, with 96 of these cases referred to relevant institutions, including referrals to Regional Technical Unit, legal aid institutions, and women’s crisis centres.

INKLUSI’s CSO partners are supporting local governments and schools in Indonesia to improve access to and quality of education for students with disability. ‍ BaKTI and its local CSO partners support 7 local governments to accelerate implementation of the national government’s Inclusive Education initiative. They built local government and school awareness and capacity in inclusive education, provided technical assistance to develop required legal frameworks and assess schools. Fifty schools were selected to pilot this initiative at the early childhood, primary and junior high school levels. As a result, 3 local governments are passing regulations mandating schools to accept and be inclusive of students with disability. Supported by CSO partners, local departments of education started delivering training for principals and teachers in inclusive education and established 4 local government Disability Services Units for Education to lead inclusive education efforts. ‍ These efforts led to schools formally identifying and accepting students with disability, teachers ‍ gaining a better understanding of different types of disability and adapting their teaching methods to meet diverse learning needs. A school have invested in assistive devices (such as reading glasses and wheelchairs) and upgraded their infrastructure accessibility. This is creating a more supportive learning environment for students with disability.

INKLUSI’s CSO partners have established and strengthened community-based groups to respond to cases of gender and domestic violence. These groups have been equipped with knowledge on gender equality, sexual and gender-based violence. They serve as the first point of response before referring survivors to other services. ‍ During the reporting period, these community-based groups supported 871 victim-survivors of violence—including domestic and gender-based violence—to access various services. These included receiving in-person and/or online reports, providing psychosocial counselling, offering shelter, accompanying victims for medical examinations and health services, and delivering legal assistance such as legal advice and court accompaniment. Victims were also referred to integrated government services, including the Regional Technical Implementation Unit for the Protection of Women and Children (UPTD PPA). Some community-based groups have formal arrangements with UPTD PPA to make it easier to refer cases. ‍ INKLUSI’s CSO partners also established and/or strengthened 13 UPTD PPA, as well as 6 taskforces to prevent and respond to sexual violence in private and state university campuses. INKLUSI’s community groups play a critical role in bridging between communities and government services, especially given UPTD PPA are often under-resourced and under-funded.

INKLUSI’s partnership with SIGAB, an Indonesian Organisations of People with Disability (OPD), marks an important milestone for this OPD- this is the first time they become a national partner in a development project, which is having positive effects on the broader disability community. INKLUSI supported SIGAB transitioned into a grant-making organisation and strengthened its financial systems, enhancing its ability to partner with and support local OPDs. ‍ Through INKLUSI, SIGAB works with 5 local OPDs that have established 62 Village Disability Groups (KDD). These groups play an active role in local development planning and policy and have established district-level forums for joint advocacy. KDDs supported the development of 30 inclusive village regulations, promoting more inclusive and accessible communities for people with disability. KDDs continue to attract government funding and advocate for better access to basic services. to promote economic empowerment, KDDs established 76 businesses involving 250 members, providing opportunities for people with disabilities to gain skills and improve their livelihoods. ‍ At the national and district levels, SIGAB strengthened policy engagement by supporting OPDs and KDDs to contribute to the development of national and local disability action plans, inclusive village regulations, and advocacy for disability-inclusive elections at both national and local levels.

KAPAL Perempuan, a women’s rights organisation, is one of INKLUSI’s 11 CSO national partners. With INKLUSI’s funding, capacity-building and convening support, KAPAL Perempuan expanded its influence nationally and locally by establishing and strengthening 30 Sekolah Perempuan (Women’s Schools) to build women’s leadership and empowerment. ‍ Sekolah Perempuan is recognised through Village Government Decrees. They enable women to participate meaningfully in village development planning and policy, and access public funding. These schools successfully advocated funding for marginalised groups and their own operations to promoting inclusion. Some have established cooperatives to support financial sustainability. ‍ KAPAL Perempuan connected grassroots women’s voices to national and district policymakers through catalysing Indonesia’s first national women’s consultation with the National Development Planning Agency (Bappenas) and Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and Child Protection (MOWECP). KAPAL Perempuan and other INKLUSI CSO partners used these findings to successfully advocate for the integration of GEDSI principles into Indonesia’s 2025-2045 National Long-Term Development Plan, and formal adoption of the national women’s consultation by MOWECP. KAPAL Perempuan was critical in advancing establishment of MOWECP’s Women’s Empowerment Service Institutions – a national policy framework inspired by the Sekolah Perempuan model to improve quality of life and participation of women in development.

PERMAMPU, one of INKLUSI’s 11 CSO national partners, is a consortium of 8 local women’s CSOs from across Sumatra. With INKLUSI’s flexible funding, capacity-building and networking opportunities, PERMAMPU has strengthened and expanded its work empowering grassroots women across Sumatra. They established and strengthened 82 Credit Unions (CU) serving 1,938 women members. CU loans provide direct benefits for women, such as business capital and education support. More than just financial institutions, CUs have become political spaces for grassroots women—where they learn to manage money, discuss social issues, and understand rights related to reproductive health and protection from violence. Many CU members are becoming active in their communities, especially as cadres in PERMAMPU’s One Stop Services and Learning centres, providing important education on reproductive health, prevention of child marriage and prevention and handling cases of violence. Some are also active in policy advocacy. Through savings and collective decision-making in meetings, CUs strengthen leadership and participatory democracy. ‍ INKLUSI enabled PERMAMPU to develop its new Gaharu Family initiative, which is helping to shift power relations within households and promote gender equality values. This layered approach—economic, social, political, and personal—has helped improve the position of women in socially and culturally complex regions.

PR Yakkum, an organisation advocating for the rights of people with psychosocial disabilities (and one of INKLUSI’s 11 national partners), has expanded its reach and impact through INKLUSI’s flexible funding, capacity-building and networking support. Applying an intersectionality lens, PR Yakkum is reaching the most marginalised groups and strengthening its role as an intermediary organisation. ‍ With INKLUSI’s support, PR Yakkum revised its internal structures and strengthened sub-granting arrangements for 5 local CSOs, building their capacity to support people with psychosocial disabilities, apply intersectional approaches, and strengthen policy advocacy, financial management, and monitoring, evaluation and learning. Through facilitated organisational capacity assessments, PR Yakkum is supporting these 5 local CSO partners to develop tailored plans to strengthen their own organisations. ‍ These partnerships have expanded PR Yakkum’s grassroots disability networks. Local CSO partners established 19 self-help groups that empower people with disability. During the reporting period, these groups enabled 116 instances of people with disability participating in local government and community activities, 919 instances of people with disability accessing government services and 17 businesses established involving 157 people with disability. ‍ PR Yakkum also strengthened their national and district networks, enabling them to connect local voices with policymakers to inform disability policy.

Through flexible funding and technical assistance, INKLUSI supported CSO partners to assist 14,805 marginalised people (6,710 men and 8,095 women), including people with disabilities (2,281 men, 2,378 women), to access social protection including national health insurance, Indonesia’s Health Card, direct cash assistance, food assistance and the Family Hope Program. They have done this through establishing and building the capacity of community-based groups that provide social protection referral mechanisms, with CSO partners directly facilitating marginalised people to access social protection. ‍ For example, PEKKA’s Community Based Service Clinics (KLIK PEKKA) collaborate with local government agencies to attend local clinics that directly handle access and service delivery complaints from women, people with disabilities and other marginalised communities, including related to accessing social protection. This led to 1,641 instances of marginalised people accessing government social protection programs during this period as a direct result of our intervention.

Through flexible grant funding and technical assistance, INKLUSI has enabled its local CSO partners to support 11,453 women entrepreneurs (including 379 women with disability) to establish and strengthen businesses and cooperatives through a community-based economic empowerment approach. These women—including elderly women, survivors of violence, and persons with disabilities—have started and/or already developed both individual and group businesses. The support provided through INKLUSI includes skills training for production, business development coaching, financial literacy education, and facilitation of business licensing. Additional economic stimulus was also provided through access to equipment, raw material and livestock to reinforce business capital. ‍ As these enterprises evolved, some of them have transitioned toward expansion and innovation. Individual and group enterprises—many of which emerged from earlier training programs—have now become actively engaged in productive ventures, including food processing, handicrafts, eco-batik production, and livestock farming. Several partners have also guided the transformation of semi-informal business groups, such as savings and loans, into cooperatives. These cooperatives serve as vital platforms for marketing, distribution, and financial services, including savings and credit. Collaboration with village and sub-district governments has helped ensure the long-term sustainability of women-led businesses.

Under the Australia–Indonesia Partnership Towards an Inclusive Society (INKLUSI) program, Australia providedfunding to five Indonesian national-level women’s CSOs that collaborated with 71 local women’s CSOs. INKLUSI enabled the national CSOs to strengthen organisational capacity, enhancing their ability to strengthen local CSOs and empower marginalised people.
These women’s CSOs supported the establishment of 174 community groups that helped 5,127 marginalised people access a range of public services, for example, in relation to legal identity documentation and in cases of violence. Through their support, these CSOs also enabled 15,624 marginalised people, including 12,347 women and 3,272 men (also comprising 308 people with disability), to have direct access to government social protection programs. The CSOs also supported the engagement of 1,349 women and 130 men (including 44 people with disability) in public policy processes, enabling them to influence decisions that affected them. Furthermore, 268 businesses and cooperatives were established, involving 3,190 women and 12 men (including five people with disability).
